profiles.meeting_scenario: Riverside Medical Center is launching a standardized preoperative screening workflow for elective hip and knee arthroplasty patients before an increase in orthopedic OR volume next month. In this planning meeting, the director of the preoperative assessment clinic and the anesthesia lead for the orthopedic service are aligning on how patients will be screened, what information will be collected, how risk findings will be communicated to surgeons and anesthesiologists, and when each step should happen relative to the scheduled operation. The agenda is to set the clinic timeline, define what gets included in the shared pre-op documentation, decide how high-risk cases are escalated, and confirm what counts as a patient being ready to proceed. The expected outcome is a workable pilot process, with each side leaving believing they have agreed on responsibilities and timing for the new pathway.

members.name: Dr. Lena Patel
members.expertise: Perioperative medicine, medical risk stratification, optimization of chronic disease before surgery
members.background: An internist and former hospitalist who built the hospital's centralized pre-op clinic and is known for reducing unnecessary testing while keeping cancellation rates low.
members.private_state: She wants a lean, evidence-based workflow that her clinic can absorb without extra staffing, and she is especially concerned about avoiding blanket testing or manual coordination work that will slow clinic throughput.
hidden_assumptions: "Optimized" means modifiable medical issues have been addressed enough that surgery can proceed safely with a documented plan, even if every consultant recommendation is not fully completed before the case date.
"Recent labs" for stable arthroplasty patients usually means results already available within the last 3-6 months unless there has been a clinical change.
A signed pre-op note plus an EHR message to the surgeon's pool is the standard and sufficient way to communicate risk findings and needed perioperative adjustments.
"Sharing the pre-op packet" means placing her assessment note, test summary, and recommendations in the chart; downstream teams can open linked outside records themselves if needed.

members.name: Dr. Evan Brooks
members.expertise: Regional anesthesia, perioperative workflow for joint replacement programs, day-of-surgery readiness
members.background: A fellowship-trained anesthesiologist who oversees anesthesia planning for the joint replacement service line and focuses on preventing same-day delays caused by missing information or unresolved medical issues.
members.private_state: He wants zero surprises on the day before surgery, with anesthesia-ready charts that do not require his team to chase records, clarify medication plans, or discover unresolved consultant recommendations at the last minute.
hidden_assumptions: "Optimized" means all follow-up items that could materially change anesthesia planning have already been completed and documented before the case is treated as ready.
"Recent labs" for older joint-replacement patients means values close enough to the surgery date, typically within about 30 days, so they reflect current renal function, hemoglobin, and electrolytes.
"Flagging surgery" means active verbal or operational escalation to the scheduler and pre-op/OR workflow, not just passive documentation in the EHR.

"Sharing the pre-op packet" includes a curated bundle of key outside cardiology or pulmonary records and clear medication instructions, not merely a clinic note with references to documents elsewhere in the chart.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members talk about getting patients 'optimized' before surgery.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes a patient is optimized once major modifiable risks have been identified, addressed as far as practical, and accompanied by a documented perioperative plan, even if some recommendations remain pending.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes a patient is optimized only when all clinically relevant follow-up tasks likely to affect anesthesia management are completed and the chart is effectively final for scheduling purposes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term is common, positive, and routine in perioperative discussions, so both hear alignment in principle and neither thinks to unpack the threshold hidden inside the word.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members agree that joint patients should have 'recent labs' available.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means prior CBC and BMP from the last several months are acceptable for clinically stable patients without interval changes, with new testing ordered only when history or exam suggests it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means labs close to the surgery date, especially within roughly 30 days for older arthroplasty patients, because anesthesia wants near-current hemoglobin, creatinine, and electrolyte values.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse the same apparent safety principle, and 'recent' sounds sufficiently precise in everyday hospital talk that the hidden cutoff never gets surfaced.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members say they will 'flag' high-risk patients to surgery.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes flagging means placing the concern prominently in the pre-op note and sending an EHR in-basket message to the surgeon's team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes flagging means an active escalation step, such as direct communication to the scheduler or perioperative operations workflow so the case appears on the day-before review list.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are discussing communication rather than treatment decisions, 'flagging' feels like a settled operational shorthand, and each assumes the other's workflow uses the same mechanism.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'pre-op packet'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both members refer to sending or reviewing the 'pre-op packet' before surgery.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the packet consists of her clinic assessment, problem list, relevant test results, and recommendations documented in the EHR.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the packet includes not only the assessment note but also selected outside consult records, scanned test reports, and a clearly packaged medication or device plan that anesthesia and pre-op nursing can use directly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both picture a familiar bundle of pre-op information and assume the other person means the standard packet used in their own workflow, so the boundary of what is inside the packet remains implicit.

turns.inner_thought: We need something the clinic can actually absorb before ortho volume ramps up. If this turns into blanket testing, record chasing, and custom outreach on every patient, throughput will crater. I want a standardized pathway that uses our current template, keeps the work evidence-based, and lets us move patients through efficiently without adding staff.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. With the joint service increasing volume next month, I'd like us to leave today with a workable screening pathway for elective hips and knees—who gets seen when, what goes into the shared documentation, how we communicate risk findings, and what the handoff looks like before surgery.

turns.inner_thought: My biggest concern is eliminating day-before surprises. For these joint cases, 'optimized' means the chart is truly anesthesia-ready: no dangling consult recommendations, no unresolved medication questions, no missing studies that could change planning. If we're going to scale volume, I need a process where my team is not discovering loose ends at final review.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From the anesthesia side, the main objective is fewer day-of-surgery surprises and making sure these joint patients are optimized before they hit final anesthesia review.

turns.inner_thought: Two to three weeks should be enough for us to assess risk, address modifiable issues, and document a perioperative plan without creating unnecessary extra visits. Once my note is signed and the chart is closed, the packet is there in the EHR—the assessment, summarized results, and recommendations. I do not want my team manually assembling separate bundles for downstream review.
turns.utterance: I think the cleanest timeline is for the clinic to see most patients about two to three weeks before the operation. Then once the chart is closed, we'll share the pre-op packet so the downstream teams have what they need with enough lead time.

turns.inner_thought: If the packet lands early and is complete, my team can review it before the day-before crunch. For higher-risk patients, I want them actively visible to surgery operations and scheduling so they don't disappear until the final list is built. I assume the packet will be a usable bundle, not a note that sends us hunting through the chart.
turns.utterance: Yes, that timing would help. If the pre-op packet is in early enough, my team can review it ahead of time, and any higher-risk cases can be flagged to surgery before the block is finalized.

turns.inner_thought: I need to reinforce that we are not going to order routine labs on every stable arthroplasty patient just because surgery is coming up. If they already have CBC and chemistries from the past few months and nothing has changed, that's usually fine. New testing should be driven by history, exam, or known disease, not habit.
turns.utterance: On testing, I'd prefer we stay with a focused approach rather than blanket testing. For stable patients, we'll rely on recent labs unless the history or exam suggests something has changed.

turns.inner_thought: Focused testing is fine in principle, but for older arthroplasty patients I need hemoglobin, creatinine, and electrolytes that actually reflect where they are near the case date—ideally within about 30 days. And if there are optimization items, I need them settled before the week of surgery, not documented as pending with a plan to figure it out later.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable to me, as long as recent labs are available for the older joint patients and any optimization issues are settled before the week of surgery.

turns.inner_thought: For anticoagulation, device checks, or likely OSA, my clinic can document the perioperative plan clearly in the note and communicate it through our usual channels. If the major risk issues are addressed enough to proceed safely, I will mark the patient optimized even if every downstream recommendation isn't fully completed yet. And from my perspective, flagging surgery means the note is clear and the surgeon's team gets an in-basket message.
turns.utterance: Right, and for common issues like anticoagulation plans, pacemaker checks, or probable OSA, we'll document the plan in the note, mark the patient optimized when appropriate, and flag surgery from the clinic side.

turns.inner_thought: Good—if those cases are flagged, they should surface in the workflow my team and the schedulers are already watching. And for anything tied to a cardiology or pulmonary question, I expect the packet to include the relevant outside material and the medication plan in a way that is ready to use. I do not want anesthesia nurses clicking through tabs and scanned media the day before surgery.
turns.utterance: That'll help, because then my team can pick up those flagged cases in their workflow. And I assume the pre-op packet will include any outside cardiology or pulmonary records tied to that plan.

turns.inner_thought: Best to keep this simple and build off what already exists. I'll adapt our current EHR template rather than invent a separate arthroplasty workflow. If we pilot with next Monday's list, we can see where the friction points are without committing extra manual labor up front. The packet, as far as I'm concerned, will be whatever is documented in the chart through that template.
turns.utterance: That's fine. I can build this off the clinic's current EHR template and we can pilot it starting with next Monday's hip and knee patients from the joint service.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the clinic packets start coming in, I'll tell anesthesia and the schedulers that those charts can move into routine review once they're optimized. In my mind that means they're effectively final and usable without back-and-forth. This should reduce last-minute scrambling if everyone treats the packet as the ready signal.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll alert the anesthesia team and the schedulers that once the clinic packets are in, optimized patients should be ready for routine anesthesia review.
